title: Whole-plant synthetic genome construction and rewriting

concept.text: The innovation would be the construction of a designed plant nuclear genome that supports development into a fertile, sexually reproducing plant. Researchers would specify DNA sequences and chromosome organization, assemble the designed DNA, introduce it into plant cells, establish functional chromosomes, and regenerate plants whose genome structure and inheritance could be verified. The supplied review describes computational design, modular DNA assembly, transformation, targeted integration, verification, regeneration and phenotypic validation as components of this workflow.

The proposed endpoint combines substantial or complete nuclear-genome synthesis with deliberate chromosome-scale rewriting. A convincing implementation would report how much of the nuclear genome was synthesized, identify retained native regions, and connect a designed change to a reproducible biological effect. Here, whole-plant functionality means that the reconstructed nuclear genome supports the organism through development and reproduction. Synthesis of the plant's organellar genomes would be an additional scope choice.

significance.text: Successful construction and functional rewriting would make chromosome-scale organization experimentally programmable in a multicellular plant. Researchers could build alternative genomic arrangements and compare their effects on development, chromosome behavior and inheritance. Such experiments could help determine which arrangements are necessary for normal function and which tolerate redesign. This conditional scientific value follows from the review's stated aim of understanding genome function through synthesis, redesign and phenotypic validation.

As a synthesis of the proposed capability, its revolutionary consequence would be the ability to test whole-genome design hypotheses in living, reproducing plants. Constructing a functioning genome would establish that a particular design works under the conditions tested. Predicting useful traits, improving agricultural performance and transferring designs across species would require additional understanding of gene regulation, development and environmental responses. The ability to manufacture a genome would therefore leave substantial work in predicting the organism it produces.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is an end-to-end route from a designed plant nuclear genome to verified, functional chromosomes in a regenerated fertile plant. Each stage must preserve the intended sequence and organization while yielding cells capable of development. The June 2025 review specifically identifies accurate integration of large DNA fragments as a technical bottleneck in seed-plant synthetic genomics, connecting DNA construction to the difficulty of installing the resulting material correctly.

Additional proposed engineering requirements include assembling large, repetitive chromosomes, establishing centromeres and other essential chromosome functions, and maintaining chromosome stability through cell division and reproduction. The supplied preview does not provide enough substantive detail to assess solutions to these requirements. Their inclusion describes the intended functional challenge and preserves questions raised in the research.

A further proposed biological requirement is compatibility between the redesigned nuclear genome and the plant's organellar genomes. The resulting organism would also need coordinated development and fertility. The supplied preview supports regeneration and phenotypic validation as workflow components, while leaving the specific nuclear–organellar constraints and the evidence for achieving fertility unresolved. A successful design would have to establish these functional properties experimentally.

current_state.text: Lan, Chen, Wang and Jiao published Genome synthesis in plants on 25 June 2025. The retained publisher preview contains substantive abstract and key-point text describing plant-genome redesign, synthesis and the associated experimental workflow. It also identifies accurate large-fragment integration as a remaining bottleneck specifically in seed plants at that publication date. The full review body and substantive figures were unavailable in the supplied review materials.

The preview characterizes the 2024 study by Chen and colleagues, A designer synthetic chromosome fragment functions in moss, as the first demonstration of partial chromosome-arm synthesis in plants. This establishes that the review reports a dated partial achievement in moss. The primary study's methods, results and figures were not supplied for inspection, so its experimental scope and the review's priority characterization could not be independently assessed. The supplied evidence gives no verified fragment length, synthesized genome fraction, fertility outcome or inheritance measurements for that study.

The earlier research recorded a sign-in failure during a publisher-page recheck. The subsequently retained artifact contains substantive subscription-preview text, including the chromosome-arm report and integration bottleneck. That partial access supports the qualified statements above. It leaves the full review and the underlying primary experiment unavailable for validation.

A complete synthetic nuclear genome supporting a fertile plant is unestablished by the supplied evidence. The empty freshness record leaves field-wide status as of 1 November 2026 unresolved. Although the source index records retrieval of the publisher artifact on 11 November 2026, its scientific account dates to June 2025. The retrieval date alone cannot establish subsequent progress or continued absence of a completed plant.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Produce a fertile plant capable of sexual reproduction with a substantially or wholly synthesized nuclear genome. Report the synthesized fraction, identify every retained native region, and explain the operational meaning of substantial synthesis for that experiment. These are proposed criteria for evaluating the innovation. The supplied evidence provides no consensus numerical threshold.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed structural and inheritance verification. Independently verify the intended chromosome sequences and organization, document unintended changes, and establish that the designed chromosomes persist through plant development and sexual transmission. Report chromosome stability, fertility and inheritance across the generations actually examined. Verification should make clear which essential chromosome functions were demonstrated and which regions or functions continue to depend on retained native material.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional and reproducibility test. Introduce a deliberate chromosome-scale redesign with a stated predicted effect, compare the resulting plants with appropriate controls, and reproduce the effect in independently generated plants. Independent replication would strengthen the claim that the construction and its biological consequence are reproducible. Reporting unsuccessful constructions and variability would help define the reliability of the method.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries. Specify the plant species, regeneration conditions, tested environments, generations followed and extent of nuclear–organellar compatibility demonstrated. Report the resources and construction effort required so that practical feasibility can be assessed. Tests across a finite set of species, designs and environments would establish the breadth demonstrated within that set. Broader transferability would remain an empirical question.

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. BOT-04, An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants, addresses enabling operations that could make synthetic-genome installation and plant recovery more accessible. BOT-03 adds the challenge of constructing and validating designed nuclear chromosomes at genome scale. BOT-05, Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance, would help select designs and predict their consequences. BOT-03 could supply controlled genome-scale perturbations for testing those predictions.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-14, Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits, overlaps with the need to establish functional chromosome states and stable inheritance after reconstruction. It centers on inherited regulatory states, while BOT-03 centers on genome construction and sequence organization. BOT-06, Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major crop families, could help preserve particular engineered genotypes. BOT-03's proposed completion test specifically includes sexual reproduction and verified chromosome transmission.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-12, A causal map of plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control, BOT-13, A predictive mechanism for plant cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing, and BOT-17, Predictive control of plant cell-division planes and tissue patterning, address mechanisms that shape whole-plant function and development. Their findings could inform synthetic-genome designs, and chromosome-scale redesign could provide experiments to probe those mechanisms. Each retains its own mechanistic objective beyond demonstrating a functioning synthetic nuclear genome.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-01, Nitrogen-fixing partnerships for major cereal crops, BOT-02, A functional carbon-concentrating photosynthetic system in rice, and BOT-16, Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange, concern specific metabolic or symbiotic capabilities. Genome synthesis could eventually provide a platform for coordinated changes relevant to these goals. Achieving each capability would still require its own biological design and functional evidence.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-07, Transferable resurrection-like desiccation tolerance in productive crops, BOT-08, Programmable, durable plant immunity against diverse pathogens, BOT-10, Plants that reliably deposit durable additional carbon in soil, and BOT-15, Broadly transferable perennial grain production, describe possible targets for complex plant redesign. Their success would require evidence for the particular trait, its durability and its performance under relevant conditions. A synthetic-genome plant would create opportunities to investigate these targets without establishing their achievement.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-09, Affordable preservation and recovery of exceptional plant diversity, overlaps with the capacity to recover functional plants from stored biological information or material. Its preservation objective includes diversity that a particular synthetic nuclear-genome design may only partly capture. BOT-11, A testable causal explanation for the early radiation of flowering plants, addresses an evolutionary explanation. Synthetic-genome experiments could potentially test selected hypotheses about genomic organization or function, while the historical explanation would require its own comparative and causal evidence.

change_log.change: Preserved BOT-03 and its title, and clarified the endpoint as nuclear-genome construction supporting a fertile whole plant.
change_log.reason: The concept concerns nuclear-genome synthesis. Whole-plant function does not require synthesis of every organellar genome.

change_log.change: Integrated the documented design-to-regeneration workflow with the original chromosome-function and compatibility challenges.
change_log.reason: The preview supports the core workflow and seed-plant integration bottleneck. Repetitive-chromosome assembly, centromere function and nuclear–organellar compatibility remain proposed requirements whose details are unresolved.

change_log.change: Replaced the blanket access limitation with an account of the substantive retained subscription preview.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies accessible text supporting the partial chromosome-arm report and integration bottleneck. Full-review and primary-study access limitations still affect interpretation.

change_log.change: Attributed the 2024 partial chromosome-arm achievement in moss to the June 2025 review and retained the primary-study validation limitation.
change_log.reason: The preview supports this attribution but supplies insufficient evidence to independently establish experimental scope, quantitative results or priority.

change_log.change: Separated the dated evidence from unresolved November 2026 field status.
change_log.reason: A June 2025 review and a later retrieval timestamp cannot establish current completion or field-wide absence of a completed plant.

change_log.change: Expanded completion proposals to include synthesis coverage, retained native regions, independent verification, reproducibility and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These make the proposed endpoint assessable while preserving uncertainty about thresholds and transferability.

change_log.change: Expanded conditional significance and mapped relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Genome construction could enable causal experiments and future trait engineering, while prediction, specific traits and related scientific objectives retain separate evidentiary requirements.

unresolved_issues: The primary 2024 moss study remains unavailable in the supplied materials. Fragment size, synthesis coverage, chromosome behavior, fertility, inheritance and the priority claim require primary-study assessment.

The full June 2025 review and substantive figures remain unavailable. The retained preview cannot resolve the detailed treatment of repetitive DNA, centromeres, fertility or nuclear–organellar compatibility.

The supplied freshness record contains no subsequent evidence establishing whether a complete synthetic nuclear genome in a fertile plant had been achieved by 1 November 2026 or by the artifact's retrieval on 11 November 2026.
No numerical threshold for a substantially synthesized nuclear genome is supplied. Any demonstration would need to disclose its coverage and retained native regions.
Reliable transfer across plant species, construction efficiency and the ability to predict useful whole-plant traits remain unestablished by the supplied evidence.
